paragraphs.text: ON OUR HOLY FATHER EPHRAEM. What moves me to the present subject is the parable in the divine Gospels, the mystical teaching of the lamp. It frees my tongue, which was enslaved under the muzzle of speechlessness. It levels the roads of thought in advance, like tracks for horses, and the many-formed chariot of discourse is made ready to run along a highway, as the parable cries out clearly somewhere in these words: “They do not light a lamp and put it under the bushel, but on the lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house.” And it adds the deeper meaning of this, saying: “So let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works.” It would be blameworthy, then, to hide ourselves and be timid in matters where the Master himself has told us to take courage. He has kindled, as it were, a bright torch, brighter than the sun's: the life of our divine Father that is now set before us to be told. He does not want this life hidden under the bushel of silence. He wants it set up high on the very summit of the Church, so that it may shine on all who move about in the house of this world, and so that those who see it may glorify the Father who is in heaven. So we need not be too scrupulous about that father's binding injunction, since by keeping it the Master's ordinance would be trampled underfoot. Indeed, we must take the starting point of our praises from that injunction, even if in the present treatment it has been placed after the praises. For to someone who knows how to judge matters rightly, that injunction is not simply a bond that keeps us from crowning with praise a man who turned away from human glory. Rather, it is a bond that does not bind, a restraint that cannot restrain, and it pushes those who love him toward the opposite. For by the very means through which he aimed to escape our praises, walling off the attempt with a binding injunction, we

find the occasions for our praises. Each of his excellences gives occasion for complete praise, but above all the fact that he took no pleasure in praise. For he wished not to seem good, but to be good. For this reason alone, even if he had done nothing else worthy of praise, it is right that he be praised: he so firmly bade farewell to praises that he even sealed his rebuke of them with a binding injunction. For us, this is what first opens the racecourse of our discourse. It assures us that we are not going aimlessly or being carried over a cliff, but are traveling the royal road, once we reason correctly that if this wondrous man of God had not seen that he was worthy of praise, he would not have forbidden those who wished to speak well of him. For no one who is not admired for the greatest excellences charges those who come after him, while he is still alive, to let his memory vanish into the pit of oblivion. Besides this, one may also say the following. Paul, the orator of grace, the one who led the Church as a bride to Christ, the mouth of Christ, did not lose the title of Apostle by saying, “I am not worthy to be called an apostle.” Rather, by this very modesty he won greater renown. In the same way our great Father judged himself unworthy of praise out of reverence, and so, as a consequence, he will be found worthy of it. Our Church's law knows how to crown the zealous followers of virtue by recounting its various forms, and especially those who have been spiritually exalted through humility of mind, as the Lord said in the Gospels somewhat in these words: “He who humbles himself will be exalted.” So those who record the virtues of this God-bearing Father, and raise up his life for us as a breathing, living monument, are entirely free from blame, from mockery and from condemnation itself. The wise listener will see that what has been promised is true when, after the discourse, he gathers up the various forms of his virtues. From these we will fashion, as it were, a single crown set in gold and adorned all round with precious stones of many kinds, and we will bring it as a longed-for gift to the bride of Christ, the Church. For she rejoices to be honored with such gifts whenever the yearly memorial of the righteous comes round. Now the course of time has brought Ephraem round to be praised. How could she not welcome his memorial with great joy? Ephraem, whose name is on the lips of all Christians! Ephraem the Syrian, I mean, for I am not ashamed of the people of a man whose ways I glory in. Ephraem, the radiance of whose life and contemplation shone out over all the earth! He is known to nearly everything under the sun, and is unknown only among those to whom the great luminary of the Church, Basil,

is also unknown. Ephraem, truly the spiritual Euphrates of the Church! Watered by him, the whole body of the faithful yields the seed of faith a hundredfold. Ephraem, the fruitful vine of God, which blossoms with the fruits of teaching like sweet clusters of grapes, and gladdens the nurslings of the Church with the abundance of divine love! Ephraem, the good and faithful steward of grace, who measures out the teachings of the virtues to his fellow servants in due proportion, and manages the Master's household excellently! We have judged it superfluous to bring forward his family, his homeland, the distinction of his ancestors, the renown of his parents, his birth, his upbringing, his growth to maturity, his bodily abilities, his fortune, his skills, and the other grand themes that secular writers collect for their praises. For we have not received the custom of praising divine men on such grounds, even though he has abundant claim to praise on these counts too. Rather, let us bind on him the crown of our discourse from the things by which he made himself illustrious in life and in word. For praise belongs to what is in our own power, and rewards belong to what we freely choose. For the things listed above, blame is unreasonable and praise unfitting. How could he accept being praised for his family, when he loathed all worldly nobility and strove to become a child of God by taking up the best works? Or how could he be extolled for his homeland, when he reckoned the whole earth foreign to himself and turned away from material creation as hostile, for the sake of the eternal blessedness laid up in heaven? And how could he take pleasure in the renown of ancestors or parents, when he trampled underfoot all attachment to the body, and was weighed down even by the soul's own tunic, that is, the flesh, finding it an obstacle in the swiftest races of virtue? And how could he possibly wish to be praised for his bodily growth and way of life, or his abilities, or his skill, or any other contemptible occupation of this life? From his earliest years he was nourished and grew up in the study of the divine Scriptures. He was watered by the ever-flowing channels of grace, and he attained, to speak with the Apostle, to the measure of the stature of Christ. We know, then, that our great Father does not rejoice in being magnified by the laughable praises that please the worldly. So let us try, even if only modestly, to extol him on the basis of his own labors, for speech by its nature cannot stretch beyond its power. We do not want speechlessness to fetter our longing, nor do we want to walk a path foreign to the Fathers and slip from the royal road by running along byways. So we will craft our discourse with moderation. What are the things of his from which we have proposed to weave our praise? Practice and contemplation, which are followed by the swarm of particular virtues: faith, hope, love,

piety toward God, study of the divine Scriptures, purity of soul and body, unceasing tears, life in the desert, withdrawal from place to place, flight from harmful things, unceasing teaching, unremitting prayer, fasting and vigils without measure, sleeping on the ground and hardship beyond words, poverty and humility carried to the extreme, almsgiving that lifted him above human nature, godly zeal against those who rage against true religion, and, in short, everything that can mark a man as a man of God. With such praises our Father is adorned. He knows what is said, he understands his own excellences, and he welcomes these words as bringing benefit, not to himself, but to us, since even the mere mention of his name becomes an incentive to virtue for the earnest. For we have learned these things from no other source than what he himself sowed in his writings about himself. From these, like the praiseworthy bee gathering what is useful from many flowers, we have made this spiritual honeycomb. And he will surely not be angry with us for the attempt, since he no longer fears the evil demon, who has tripped up many even at the very end of their contests. Once he had reached the waveless harbors of the bodiless powers, he was beyond storm and surge. Come, then, let us spend a little time discussing each of the things listed, and show those gathered here what kind of man this wondrous one was, and to what height of spiritual ascent he attained. In faith he was entirely orthodox, never leaning anywhere away from true religion, as we have learned both from his writings and from the esteem in which the Church holds him. For he loathed equally the irrational confusion of Sabellius and the frenzied division of Arius. He stood within the bounds of true religion. He distinguished the one, unconfused and all-holy Trinity in number, but joined it in essence, so that he could neither be reproached, like the Jews, with an impoverished godhead, nor be carried away, like the Greeks, into frenzy over a mob of gods. Those who have behaved like drunkards toward the incomprehensible Trinity are proven to have fallen into these errors. The irrational doctrine of Apollinarius he rejected so firmly that he made every effort to drive it out of every Christian soul. Moreover, with many arguments drawn from reason and from Scripture he stopped the unguarded mouths of the Anomoeans, leaving us his God-taught words as the greatest security. If anyone wishes to see the defeat of the most audacious Novatus, let him look at the fall of that adversary in his wrestling match with the words of Ephraem. There he will find that our Teacher's superior strength in argument is as great as that of a pancratiast over a boy who is weak because he is young. He did not only refute, by the right word of faith, the heresies that sprang up like tares, sown by the sower of evil, in his own time or before it. He also foresaw with prophetic eye those that would later

sprout up wickedly, and he mowed them down in advance. All his writings and poetry are full of these proofs. In this way the son of truth never strayed from the truth. His hope was in God alone, from whom come the graces of the hopes laid up for the worthy. For throughout his life he practiced in word and deed the psalm that says: “In him my heart hoped, and I was helped.” Because he hoped in the Lord in this way, mercy will surround him. Trust in the Lord makes a man like Mount Zion, and it also places the one who has it within the highest blessedness, as one may learn from the prophets themselves. David says: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.” Jeremiah says: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope; he will be like a flourishing tree beside the waters, and will send out its root toward moisture.” And Isaiah says: “The Lord is our King, the Lord is our Savior; he will save us. Behold, God is my Savior, the Lord; I will trust in him and take courage.” And blessed Paul exhorts us, saying: “Let us hold fast the promise of our hope, for he who promised us is faithful.” Turning toward this divine hope laid up for him, he despised all worldly things and longed [?] for eternal glory. Love for God and for his neighbor he kept so exactly that, as he was departing this life, he said the following himself. It is good to quote the God-bearing Father's very words, since they are better than any proof. “Never in all my life,” he says, “did I revile the Lord, and no foolish word passed my lips. In all my life I cursed no one, and I never quarreled with any believer at all.” O blessed tongue, which dared to utter such a word! It is fitting for the angels alone, because their life is immaterial and free of strife. But for us who are slaves of the flesh, it is foreign and beyond nature, and hard to achieve. You might toil long searching the lives of those famed for their virtues, but nowhere would you find such a sign of pure and spotless love as in the Father whose story we are telling. Love is the greatest of all the virtues; blessed Ephraem achieved it as no other of the Fathers did; and each will receive according to his works. We shall leave it to others to draw the conclusion from these facts, so that we may not seem to compare Fathers with Fathers. We have not cited his words for the sake of comparison, but only to set before the eyes of the many how our Ephraem, or rather the teacher of the whole world, reached the very top of the spiritual ladder of the virtues.

He made piety his trade in acquiring true wisdom, as it is said in Job: “Behold, piety is wisdom.” Through it, as we showed a little earlier in describing the purity of his faith, he ascended like Paul to the third heaven, and he has been enriched with an undying memory and lasting renown in the Church. His study of the divine Scriptures he kindled from the lamp of David, who says: “In my meditation a fire will be kindled.” For love of spiritual contemplation [?] took hold of him and raised his longing into a soaring flame. He studied the whole of Scripture, Old and New, and dwelt lovingly on such contemplations as no one else has. He interpreted all of it exactly, word by word, from the creation of the world to the last book of grace, bringing the depths of hidden meanings into the open, with the Spirit as his lamp. He not only drained the whole spiritual mixing bowl of our own God-inspired wisdom and shared it with others. He also trained himself thoroughly in the secular wisdom of the outside world, both the part concerned with eloquence and correctness of speech and the part concerned with depth of thought. Whatever was useful in it he took up, and whatever was useless he threw away, weighing both practice and contemplation on the scales of justice. He achieved purity of soul and body as far as nature allowed, or rather beyond nature, for it is a gift of grace. He never let his soul slip from the disposition that accords with right reason; he truly ruled as a king in his soul and shone with radiance in his body. The conversion of the harlot in the well-known story bears witness to what I say. The man-slaying Belial used her as bait to entice the enlightened man into wickedness, but he fell so far short of what he hoped that the adulteress herself was ranged against that overweening Evil One. She was changed by Ephraem's exhortations and rebukes and by the spell of the divine words, and was remolded for the better, so that she proved chaste instead of licentious, modest instead of shameless, and pure instead of defiled. As I eagerly set out to speak of the ever-flowing stream of his tears, I am truly moved to weep myself, for without weeping no one could sail through the ocean of his tears in words. Just as breathing is natural to all people and goes on all the time, so shedding tears was natural to Ephraem. There was no day, no night, no midnight, no hour, not the briefest moment, when his sleepless eye was seen dry, as he wept now for the common wrongdoings, now for his own, as he called them. Wisely he fed the streams of his eyes with groans, or rather drew out his groans with floods from his eyes. And the way both came forth was remarkable, for each seemed to be the cause of the other: in him tears gave birth to

groans, and groans in turn to tears, and the cause was unknown to most people. For time did not separate them. Tears always followed groans, and groans followed tears again, in a kind of circle, so that it was unclear where it began and which was the cause of the other. Anyone who reads his writings will see this. He will find him weeping not only in his discourses on repentance, character and the good life, but even in his festal sermons, where most writers usually display great joy in their words. But he was the same everywhere, and was always rich in the gift of compunction. That is why even now he calls nearly all who hear his words back to the true life. Such power does his God-inspired word possess, mingled as it is with tears. For who is so implacable or so stony of heart that, on hearing his words, he will not be softened, cast off the hardness of his character, and grieve over his own wickedness? Who is so savage in character or so beastly in his ways that, once he has listened to his soul-profiting teaching, he will not at once become kind and gentle and a lover of good in his conduct? Who delights in the pleasures of life and turns away from weeping, yet will not lament and weep after hearing only a few of his words, and come to remember the life he has lived in view of the coming retribution? “To soften a stone” [?] is what the secular proverb says of impossible things. But experience has clearly shown us that it can be done. For this divine old man persuaded souls that were hard and unyielding both to be on their guard and to submit. Who, on reading his discourse on humility, will not at once come to hate all conceit, and even proclaim himself lower than everyone? Who, on taking up his writings on love, will not be eager to face danger for the sake of love? Who, after spending time with his writings on virginity, will not strive to present himself pure to God in soul and body? Who, on poring over his writings on the judgment, that is, the second coming of Christ, will not think he is standing before that tribunal and, trembling, expect the final sentence to be pronounced against him at once? For this celebrated and most prophetic man depicted the future court of God so vividly that nothing more remains to be known, and all that is left is to learn it by the event itself and by experience. Constantly gripped by such visions of the judgment, the blessed man fled the world and the things in the world. As the Scriptures say, “he went far away in flight, and lodged in the wilderness,” attending only to himself and to God, and receiving from there his progress in the virtues. For he knew well that life in the desert frees anyone who wishes it from the tumults of the world, that its stillness makes one a companion of the angels, and that it

raises the mind, as far as is possible, to the contemplation of God. When the Spirit moved him to go from place to place, arranging this for the edification of the many, he did not disobey or resist. For he was obedient to divine commands if anyone ever was. So, like the divine Abraham when he was commanded, he left his homeland and came to the city of the Edessenes, for it was not right for the sun to stay hidden underground for long. He came for two reasons: to embrace the holy places there, and above all to meet a learned man and either receive or impart the fruit of knowledge. On this occasion, as the story goes, when he approached the city and was entering it, he met a harlot instead of the scholar he had prayed to meet. Since what he found was different from what he expected, the encounter grieved him. So he fixed his gaze on the prostitute and [?], as one cheated of his hope. She, seeing him staring at her, in turn looked at him closely. The wise man said to her: “Tell me, woman, why are you staring at me?” She answered: “It is fitting and proper for me to do so, for I was taken from you, the man. But you should not look at me, but rather at the earth, from which you were taken.” When the wise man heard this unexpected answer, he acknowledged that he had been greatly helped, and he gave great glory to the incomprehensible power of God, who gra-

Setting out from there for Caesarea in Cappadocia, guided by the Holy Spirit, he saw the great Basil, the mouth of the Church, the golden nightingale of doctrine. When the old man saw him, he began to honor him with many praises. For with the clairvoyant eye of his soul he saw a radiant dove perched on Basil's right shoulder, supplying him with words of teaching, which Basil passed on to the people. Basil, informed by the venerable dove that taught him, perceived Ephraem's arrival and recognized that he was Ephraem the Syrian. And the two were granted a timely spiritual fellowship; so the hardship of the journey proved no loss to Ephraem. The natural integrity of his life showed him how to flee harmful things. It gave him [?] foresight for the better and vigilance against the worse, so that he admitted those thoughts that were approved and pure and more profitable for choosing the good, [?] especially those that hinder the work of teaching. For Christ had generously given the divine old man the talent of the word, which above all else he was bound to deposit on the tables of the hearts of the many. He himself is seen to say this about himself: when he had only just passed the tender age of childhood, he saw in a mystical vision a very fruitful vine spring up at his tongue, and it grew so large that it fil-

…[?] the earth, and every bird of the sky that came to it was filled with food. And the vine itself, the more it was stripped and the more birds it welcomed, the richer it grew in clusters. Another man of that time, one of great spiritual insight, also bore witness about him. He said he saw a multitude of angels coming down from heaven, carrying in their hands a scroll written on the inside and on the outside. And that divine company which appeared said among themselves: “To whom, then, ought this scroll to be entrusted?” In answer some put forward this man, others that one, and others someone else, from among the chosen men of that time. Then, after weighing them, they all said: “Truly these are holy men and servants of God; yet this scroll cannot be entrusted to them.” When they had named many of the saints of that time and were satisfied with none of them, at last they agreed and said: “No one can be entrusted with this scroll except Ephrem.” And when the seer had seen this as well, so it is said, the divine angels handing the scroll to Ephrem, the man who had been shown the vision rose during the night and went to the church. There he heard Ephrem teaching with abundant speech, seasoned with grace. Understanding then the vision he had seen, he glorified God and was amazed at the rich gift of speech given to the saint. So great an abundance of wisdom had been granted him that the streams of his words never ran dry. Yet they were slow to bring his thoughts to light. This was not because his tongue was sluggish but because his reflections were so dense. His tongue could keep pace with the reflections of other men but fell short of his own contemplations. That is why the great old man himself, praying to God for relief from the unstoppable gift of words, is said to have spoken like this: “Hold back, O Master, the waves of your grace.” For the abyss of teaching surging beneath his tongue would not let him carry the waves of thought that came one after another, since his organs of speech could not keep up with so hurried a service. Nothing else interrupted his words except prayer alone. Then his words interrupted the prayer, tears interrupted the words, and prayer the tears again. He was a word of the Word, or rather, to put it more fittingly, he was in the Word, constantly occupied through all these things with the contemplation of God. He had put the body to death together with its pleasures and, through self-control, made it a slave to reason, its governor. Having tamed it beforehand by fasting, he kept it unmoved toward what was improper but firm toward what was profitable and brought salvation to the soul. Nor did the nights break off his course of virtue by beguiling him with the fantasies of sleep. They received him sober from the days, and as they passed they left him still awake. He took care over this so that the hand of the ruler of this darkness would not find him sleeping. He took only as much sleep as was enough to stay alive, so that the order of nature would not be completely

overturned and the flesh would not suffer a violent breakdown. Many things kept sleep at bay and drove it from his eyes, but above all sleeping on the ground, hard living, and every kind of bodily hardship. For by these, more than anything, the passion for sleep is naturally banished. He gained a freedom from possessions as complete as that which you hear the divine apostles had. So if anyone calls him the model of those who own nothing, he will not be wrong. We have his own sweetest and blessed words on this, which he left us as a lesson in poverty when he was about to depart for heaven. They run something like this: “Ephrem never had a purse, nor a staff, nor a bag. Nor did I acquire silver or gold, or any other possession on earth. For I heard the good King in the Gospels telling his disciples to acquire nothing on earth. That is why I have never been attached to anything of the kind.” So he despised glory and money and loved the better things above all. In this too he ran an equal race with the apostles. And what shall we say in witness of his humility? Every discourse and writing of his openly proclaims this virtue, though he himself practiced it in great abundance. When would a man stub the foot of his soul on the stone of pride or conceit, when he called up tears with tears, ate ashes like bread, kept a harsh and joyless diet, and, as the Scriptures say, mixed his drink with weeping? Or how could he, who turned away from all human glory? While he was still alive, he was distressed whenever anyone praised him. He would change from one color to another, bow his face to the ground, break into a fine sweat, and be gripped by a terrible speechlessness, as if shame had numbed his tongue. And when he was departing for the blessed and endless life, he again forbade this very thing with a stern rebuke, saying: “Do not sing a song over Ephrem, do not praise me, do not bury me in costly clothing, do not make a separate tomb for my body. For I have an agreement with God that I should lodge among strangers. I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.” So you have clear proofs in abundance of this virtue too, as of the others. As for almsgiving and compassion, the rule and law of truth will judge him not only one who practiced them but also one who taught them. Because his poverty was complete, he had nothing to give to the needy. So he practiced almsgiving by stirring others to mercy with frequent exhortations. Even apart from his appearance, his word was truly a key forged by God, opening

the treasuries of the rich and supplying what was needed to those of modest means. And his angelic look, mingled with simplicity, gentleness, and great goodness, was enough by itself, when merely seen, to move even the most pitiless to compassion and mercy. Who was so given to shamelessness that he did not blush on seeing him and become somehow more decent than he had been? Perhaps someone who hears of so many achievements will suppose that this divine man did not go deeply into the doctrines of the Church. For what leisure, I might ask, would such a man have, divided as he was among so many virtues? But his knowledge of the divine doctrines was not superficial. He did not pursue it only far enough to speak and to exhort others. He was well trained in both: in the doctrines of the Church themselves, and in the teachings that try to contradict them. The first he learned so as to practice them, the second so as to refute the heretics. For zeal moved him against the wild beasts that prey on the Church. An unwritten account of this has come down to us and shows his zeal for the truth. It goes like this. The feather-brained, or rather mindless and irrational, Apollinaris made many innovations, belched them up from his belly, and dashed off a writing that did injury to true religion, arranging it in two books. He entrusted these for safekeeping to a certain woman who, it was rumored, catered to his pleasures. When the great Ephrem learned of the writing, the wise man disguised himself as one who shared Apollinaris's opinions. He approached the woman who was keeping the profane books, introduced himself as an acquaintance, brought her blessings as if from the desert, and perhaps used some other tricks as well. Then he begged her to give him the teacher's writings for his own benefit, as he put it, so that he could readily stand up to the heretics, by which, of course, he meant us. Her mind was not enlightened, and she was deceived into thinking that he too belonged to Apollinaris's faction. So she handed over the books, asking that they be returned quickly. This great Jacob supplanted the profane Esau and took the wicked birthright of his ideas, and then he wisely slipped away. He pressed page to page and smeared the whole thing with fish glue, turning the entire book into what was like a single tablet. Because the binding was so strong, no part could be pulled away from another. Having done this to both books, he gave them back to the woman who had lent them. Being a woman and unversed in clever schemes, she saw that their outside was intact and did not examine the inside closely. Not many days later, the divine old man suggested to some of the orthodox that they invite the impious Apollinaris to a debate. He accepted the invitation and, relying on his godless books,

came on the appointed day. He declined to debate in person, claiming he was worn out by old age, and asked that his own books be brought out so that he could answer and refute through them. His fellow initiates brought the books, swaggering greatly over them. That man, grown old in evil days, the judge of injustice, took one book and tried to open it. When it would not give way, being stuck fast with the glue, he made his attempt at the middle, but it would not open there either. Having failed with the first, he went on to the second. When he saw that it too was all of a piece and would not give way at all, his face changed with shame and his soul was struck with bewilderment. He left the assembly stricken with despondency and illness, and in the end he came near to death, unable to bear the humiliation. Such was our great father and teacher Ephrem in his zeal for true religion. In some cases he showed mildness and gentleness, when there was no need for battle. In others he showed severity and sternness, especially when the faith was in danger. He handled everything wisely and as the occasion required. For this too, zeal according to God, I mean, is no less than his many fasts and tears and unceasing prayers. Indeed it is greater than they, since they confine their benefit to the one who practices them, while zeal reaches out to the common good. Sound reason tests the good hunter against fighting beasts, the good helmsman against winds blowing against the ship, the skilled physician against diseases hard to cure, and the brave soldier against a heavy enemy battle line. In the same way it tests the earnest man who is zealous for true religion at the height of danger and difficulty, to see how he will rescue himself and others from the snare. There is no kind of virtue that anyone of old ever labored at which was not also achieved by this man. His soul may be likened to a spring gushing with streams of every kind, graced with benefit, sweetness, and delight. Or to a meadow in bloom, fragrant with flowers of every kind. Or to an earthly heaven adorned with various lights. Or to a paradise such as you hear of in Eden, splendid with countless fruitful trees, except that it could not be entered by the most wicked serpent, the cause of our exile. Or to anything else beautiful and delightful that nature has honored with many and various good things. Think of the blessed soul of the great Ephrem as just such a thing, surrounded on all sides by many kinds of virtue. For this admirable man made it the study of his whole life to acquire virtue in its entirety, and he strove alone to embrace every excellence. He imitated as a priest the offering of Abel, first among the righteous, which God had chosen. Yet he offered to the Lord neither victims from the flock nor fat, but an unbloody sacrifice, the worship of the mind, in purity of life [?]

wholly burnt. He rivaled Abel in everything except being slain by a wicked murderer. Instead he escaped the snares of the demon who hates mankind, rose above the plot, and passed, like Abel, to a life without end. He emulated the hope of Enosh: he not only called on the name of the Lord God himself but also taught others to call on it with him. Like Enoch, he strove not for that wondrous removal from earth to paradise but for a passage from attachment to material things to the spirit. Like Noah, he sought not the small rescue of the human race in a wooden ark but to make his own soul secure on every side. That way he could pass unharmed through the storm of life and not lose the cargo of virtue. He imitated Abraham in many other respects too, in faith, meekness, and love for God, but especially in fleeing the world, as Abraham gave up his own land and kindred. And he took the sacrifice of the Only-begotten to mean the voluntary offering of his own body for God's sake, putting to death his members that are on earth. He imitated Isaac in a willing and untroubled death, except that it was not at a father's hands. For he sacrificed himself each day in the manner of the apostles. In body he was a whole burnt offering, as far as his intention went, but in spirit he lived, and still lives, to God through the pure offering of the body, as in the ram. He imitated Jacob in supplanting the profane Esau, that is, the father of heresies, and in taking the birthright, which is the right doctrines of the Church. He also resembled Jacob in his vision, though what he saw was not a ladder set up from earth to heaven but a pillar of fire reaching to heaven, which revealed the depth of a mystery somehow more vividly. Further, like Jacob, when he was about to depart from the body he distributed blessings to his disciples as to sons. Anyone who studies them carefully will think they belong to the great Jacob himself. He imitated Joseph above all in purity and chastity of body, but much more in giving out the word as Joseph gave out grain. He was like Moses in everything, or in most things. He too fled the sorcerer Pharaoh, dwelt in the desert, saw God as far as contemplation can reach, worked wonders, and led a people as its teacher. He outwitted the Egyptians and carried off their wealth when he captured the books of the heretics and triumphed over them. He split the sea, which is salty and undrinkable unbelief, and brought the people across, which is the orthodox community. He drowned Pharaoh's men, the godless offspring of the heretics. He routed Amalek, if you wish to call one of the heretics by that name. He received from God the law of orthodoxy and shared it with us all. On the mountain he saw the pattern of the tabernacle, not the one from Moses' time but that of the dread judgment and the order of things to come. He consecrated priests by laying down laws on the priesthood. He made water spring from the rock by causing stony hearts to drip with tears.

Like Moses, he fed the people bread from heaven. He set before everyone words of love, which strengthen every soul above all, so that it can come with confidence to the divine and mystical Bread that came from the bosom of the Father for our salvation. He gave quail when he taught us believers here below to travel through heaven by remembering God and to picture the beauties there. In short, whatever terms of contemplation you use to compare our Father's noble deeds with those of the ancients, you will find him falling short in nothing. For like Joshua son of Nun he split the Jordan when he opened the hands of the rich, which had been shut to sharing, and turned them to doing good. And he gave the people as their inheritance a land, not of the earthly promise but of the heavenly kingdom. Like Samuel, he was dedicated to God from infancy and heard a divine voice. Like the great Elijah, he made a public example of the priests of shame. He brought down spiritual fire on the sacrifice of the mind, not once but many times. And he was taken up in a fiery chariot of virtues, a charioteer not of the air but of heaven. Like Elisha, he was enriched with a double portion of the grace of the Spirit, and like the prophets he was often granted visions of God. My discourse even dares to compare him with the greatest of those born of women, the mediator between the law and grace. Like the Forerunner, he dwelt in the desert. The word of God came to him as well. He became a herald of repentance and taught those who came to him to confess their sins. Like Paul, the chosen vessel, he endured trials of every kind. He never tired of sowing the seeds of repentance, as Paul never tired of sowing the seeds of faith. But why must I compare him with individuals one by one, when his achievements fill the whole world? Since his works are plain to see, a long speech is superfluous. Length of speech even turns to the discredit of the virtues, as though they could not show themselves well enough through deeds and needed the help of words. Still, it is good to add to this discourse, like a most delightful seasoning, the much-celebrated wonder at his death. When this God-bearing man was about to depart for heaven, he charged those present that they were not allowed to bury his body in costly clothing. If anyone, out of love for his father, had planned or prepared such a thing, he must on no account carry out the plan but must give the very thing intended for the burial to the poor. One of those standing by, a prominent man, had already prepared a costly garment and had intended to bury the divine old man's body in it. When he heard the rebuke he was grieved. He put off giving the garment he had prepared to the poor, having decided in his own mind that it would be more pious to give its value to the needy instead. At once he was struck by an evil demon [?] and reaped the bitterest sheaves of his disobedience,

thrashing about in front of the saint's bed and foaming at the mouth. The most compassionate man of God said to the sufferer: “Why, man, what unreasonable thing have you done that has thrown you into this danger?” At his command the man got up, though his mind was darkened by the demon, and told his hidden thought and revealed his disobedience. When he had confessed, the most compassionate old man made him well again. He freed him from his affliction by laying on his holy hands and by prayer, and then he said to him: “Fulfil your promise, man, the one you made long ago.” Such was the marvel he worked at the end of his life. He also roused those who were with him to zeal for virtue with many exhortations, as his last discourse shows. Then he breathed his last and passed, well accepted, into the calm harbor of the eternal kingdom. Where else should we imagine his soul has come to rest, if not plainly in the heavenly dwellings? There are the ranks of angels, the choirs of prophets, the thrones of apostles, the joy of martyrs, the gladness of the saints, the splendor of teachers, the festal gathering of the firstborn, and the pure sound of those who keep the feast there. Into those good things which angels long to look into, into that holy place, went the most blessed and holy soul of our blessed and celebrated Father. I think that the virtues of his life lead the way for his soul as it ascends to heaven, and that each one shows it those unspeakable and unseen beauties. Perhaps love, the greatest of all the virtues, comes up and speaks like this: “See, dearest soul, what beauty I have won for you,” and as she speaks she points out the delight. And humility runs up and says: “Look, soul beloved by God, what a place of rest I too have prepared for you.” And so, one by one, all the virtues speak and point out the rewards that they, once labored for, have now won for that soul. O departure much praised in song and worthy of envy! O death that needs no tears! O parting that brings about the union longed for! O passing that leaves no regret to the one who passed! O funeral that holds no regret! For the very things that make us admire his way of life are the things that give us consolation. With other people death is known as a cause of tears for those left behind. But with the saints it becomes a source of gladness and festivity, because such a death is not death but rather a passing and a crossing over to better things. These praises are offered to you by us, best of Fathers and teacher of the world, with a bold tongue, like gifts beneath your worth. We do not offer them as though you needed them. For what glory can words bestow when they fall short of the worth

[?] …walking in [the footsteps] of the one being praised), but rather for the benefit of the living, since for most people the praise of good men is the greatest encouragement and incentive toward better things. Many other things moved us to these words and made us bold. I pass over your many kinds of excellence, and the fame of your life and teaching, which is talked of throughout the whole world. More than these, it was your wonderful protection and the deliverance of your namesake, the man who urged us to strip for this contest. He was carried off as a captive by barbarians, descendants of Ishmael, and was separated from his homeland for no short time. As he was returning home, not knowing which road would serve him, he met with your extraordinary guidance and was taught the road best suited to his safety, and he truly did not miss his goal. Indeed, when he had come to the very height of danger and was expecting death, hard pressed by a barbarian attack on the road, he only called upon your name, saying, "Saint Ephrem, help me!" At that he passed unharmed through the maze of dangers, scorned his fear, found a deliverance beyond understanding, and, guarded by your providence, was restored to his homeland against all hope. For this reason we have dared to speak at greater length on the matters mentioned above, and have dared to touch upon your praises with unclean lips. If our words have gone a long way toward what is fitting, we will record you as the cause of our success and acknowledge our gratitude. But if our praises fall far short of your worth, then again we will blame you as the cause of our failure, bold as the claim may be. For you wish to flee praise, and as you embraced humility while you lived, so you embrace it now that you have departed, and so you hinder those who wish to praise you. Yet whether it is this or the former, we discharge our debt as far as we are able, and we trust that you will not turn away from us, your ardent and devoted children, but will receive our babbling as parents receive the dear lisping of their children. And you, standing at the divine altar and ministering with the angels to the all-holy Trinity, the source of life, remember all of us, asking for us forgiveness of sins and the enjoyment of the eternal kingdom, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory, with the Father who is without beginning and the divine and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
